Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal

PCP (phencyclidine) and stimulants · opioids · alcohol withdrawal · benzodiazepines · cannabisWhich drug do the pupils and vital signs point to, and is it intoxication or withdrawal?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Pinpoint pupils slow breathing decreased consciousness: opioid airway first, naloxone
  • Agitation from PCP (phencyclidine), cocaine or amphetamine a benzodiazepine; no beta-blocker for cocaine
  • Alcohol: delirium tremens, usually at 48 to 72 h, can kill benzodiazepine thiamine before glucose
What it is

Intoxication: a toxidrome read from pupils breathing vital signs

Withdrawal: timed from the last dose; alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill

Driver

Stimulants: sympathomimetic surge

Opioids: act at opioid receptors; naloxone is a competitive antagonist there

Sedative withdrawal: onset and length follow half-life duration of use

Triggers

Stopping alcohol seizures generally at 6 to 48 h, delirium tremens usually at 48 to 72 h

Stopping a benzodiazepine withdrawal, 1 to 2 days after a short-acting benzodiazepine, several days to a week after a long-acting one

Cocaine even mild coronary disease can trigger acute coronary syndrome

Flumazenil in a long-term benzodiazepine user may precipitate withdrawal, occasionally seizures

Intravenous glucose before thiamine risks Wernicke encephalopathy

Chain

By time since the last drink: tremor, anxiety 6 to 24 h; hallucinosis 12 to 24 h; seizures 6 to 48 h; delirium tremens usually 48 to 72 h

PCP: psychomotor agitation hyperthermia

Cocaine: hemodynamic surge vasoconstriction can trigger acute coronary syndrome

Insights

Dilated pupils with autonomic overactivity fit a stimulant and opioid withdrawal alike; yawning and goose flesh mark withdrawal

Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill; a spontaneous opioid stop is distressing, not life-threatening

Substance by substancedetail behind the chain
PCPNystagmus (horizontal, vertical or rotary) in 60% to 90%; hypertension in 60%, tachycardia in 30%Complications: rhabdomyolysis, hypoglycemia, seizures, hypertensive crisis, coma
StimulantComplications: seizures, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, coronary or cerebral ischemia
Opioid withdrawalTearing, runny nose, goose flesh, muscle aches, diarrhea, vomiting; peaks within 48 to 72 h after heroin
SedativeSlurred speech, ataxia, unsteadiness, fine lateral-gaze nystagmus, depressed reflexes; high doses depress consciousness and breathing
CannabisRaised heart rate, nystagmus, red conjunctivae, lethargy, poor concentrationHyperemesis: cyclical vomiting usually eased by warm showers and by stopping cannabis
2Urgent risks
BreathingPinpoint pupils, slow breathing, decreased consciousness
Breathing can fail again within hours as naloxone wears off

If the opioid overdose triad is present, choose airway and ventilation, then naloxone.

AlcoholSeizures at 6 to 48 h; disorientation, hallucinations, fever, usually at 48 to 72 h
Delirium tremens: mortality 1% to 5%

If it is delirium tremens, choose an intravenous benzodiazepine, promptly.

SedativeBenzodiazepine stopped: 1 to 2 days after a short-acting benzodiazepine, several days to a week after a long-acting one
Potentially life-threatening, like alcohol withdrawal

If a dependent patient is coming off a benzodiazepine, choose a slow taper of a long-acting benzodiazepine.

HeartChest pain with agitation after cocaine
Evaluate as any possible ischemia; beta-blockers are contraindicated

If there is cardiovascular toxicity or agitation, choose a benzodiazepine first, nitrates if still needed.

HeatHyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis or seizures with PCP or a stimulant

If agitation is driving the heat, choose benzodiazepine sedation.

ReversalOversedated long-term benzodiazepine user
Flumazenil may precipitate withdrawal and occasionally seizures

If the user is long-term, choose no flumazenil.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Opioid overdoseDecreased consciousness, slow breathingPinpoint pupils with slow breathing; reverses with naloxone
Sedative overdoseSlurred speech, ataxia, decreased alertnessHigh doses: decreased consciousness and respiratory depression
Opioid withdrawalDilated pupils, autonomic overactivityFrom 4 h after heroin, slower after methadone; yawning, runny nose, goose flesh, diarrhea
Cocaine or amphetamineAgitation, sweating, tachycardiaDilated pupils, hypertension, hyperthermia; can bring coronary ischemia
PCPViolence, hallucinations, delusions, hypertensionNystagmus in any direction, vertical included
Alcoholic hallucinosisAuditory, tactile or visual hallucinationsUsually 12 to 24 h; clear consciousness, autonomic signs usually absent
Confusion, fleeting hallucinations, tremor, sweating, fever, fast pulseUsually 48 to 72 h after the last drink; mortality 1% to 5%
Benzodiazepine withdrawalLike alcohol withdrawal; potentially life-threatening1 to 2 days (short-acting) or several days to a week (long-acting) after stopping
CannabisRaised heart rate, slowed concentrationRed conjunctivae; cyclical vomiting usually eased by warm showers
Delusions or hallucinations, which PCP also causesPersists about 1 month or longer after intoxication or withdrawal ends, or began before use
Agitation and high arousal, as with a stimulantA stimulant adds dilated pupils, sweating, tachycardia and hypertension
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Vertical or rotary nystagmus with violencePCPIntravenous or intramuscular benzodiazepine
Pinpoint pupils, very slow breathingOpioid overdoseAirway, then naloxone
Chest pain, dilated pupils, sweating after cocainePossible myocardial ischemiaBenzodiazepine first; no beta-blocker
Seizure 6 to 48 h after the last drinkAlcohol withdrawal seizureBenzodiazepine; routine phenytoin unlikely to help

Pause point. The bait: a test before treatment, naloxone for any altered patient, a beta-blocker for cocaine chest pain, or hallucinosis for delirium tremens. In the bank the answer is the treatment itself (naloxone, intravenous lorazepam); midsize pupils with normal breathing are not opioid; disorientation is delirium tremens.

5Diagnostic criteria
Recognition triad: opioid overdose Pupils – pinpoint, though not in every patient · Breathing – respiratory depression · Alertness – decreased consciousness
Benzodiazepine withdrawal Onset – 1 to 2 days after a short-acting one, several days to a week after a long-acting one; can last weeks · Risk – potentially life-threatening, like alcohol withdrawal
7Treatment
1

Reversethe opioid overdose triad

Airway and ventilation, then naloxone

It can wear off before the opioid, so observe; it can precipitate withdrawal.

2

1st lineagitation from PCP, cocaine or amphetamine

A benzodiazepine, intravenous or intramuscular

Lowers central sympathetic outflow. For cocaine, nitrates if vasodilation is still needed. Guideline detailLorazepam 2 to 4 mg or diazepam 5 to 10 mg, intravenous or intramuscular

3

1st linemoderate to severe alcohol withdrawal

A benzodiazepine, symptom-triggered by a Guideline detailCIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) or SAWS (Short Alcohol Withdrawal Scale) scores set the as-needed doses

Also for seizures (not routine phenytoin) and, intravenously and promptly, delirium tremens; haloperidol not at first. With intravenous fluids, thiamine before glucose. Guideline detail100 mg intravenously, before any glucose

4

1st lineopioid withdrawal

Buprenorphine or methadone

Distressing, not dangerous, after a spontaneous stop. Guideline detailSublingual buprenorphine 4 to 12 mg to start, an alternative to methadone

5

Adjunctautonomic signs

Clonidine

Can ease autonomic signs, such as blood pressure, in opioid withdrawal; in alcohol withdrawal only as an adjunct to a benzodiazepine.

6

Avoidtempting but wrong

Flumazenil in a long-term user; urinary acidification for PCP; beta-blockers in cocaine toxicity

Flumazenil is best kept for respiratory depression during a procedure.

First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
PCP agitationBenzodiazepineNo urinary acidification: acidosis, myoglobin in the kidney
Cocaine or amphetamineBenzodiazepineNo beta-blockers in cocaine toxicity; nitrates for persistent hypertension
Opioid overdoseAirway, then naloxoneRespiratory depression can recur within hours: observe
Opioid withdrawalBuprenorphine or methadoneNot naloxone: it treats overdose
Alcohol withdrawalBenzodiazepine, symptom-triggeredThiamine before glucose
Benzodiazepine withdrawalSlow taper of a long-acting one (eg clonazepam), reported in outpatient careCan last weeks
Benzodiazepine overdoseNo routine flumazenilWithdrawal or seizures in long-term users
Cannabinoid hyperemesisStop cannabisWarm showers usually relieve it
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
After naloxoneObserve until its effect is gone; breathing can fail again within hours
Alcohol withdrawal under wayKeep dosing by symptom score; delirium tremens usually comes at 48 to 72 h
Psychosis lasts about 1 month after stoppingConsider an independent psychotic disorder
Active use, intoxication or withdrawalCount it as a modifiable suicide risk factor
Long-term care after withdrawal
Use disorderChooseWatch for
AlcoholNaltrexone; acamprosate may also lower relapseNaltrexone helps most who take it consistently; not with acute hepatitis, liver failure or opioid dependence
Alcohol, supervisedDisulfiram, best in highly motivated patientsDrinking on it: flushing, throbbing headache, tachycardia; heavy drinking may add vomiting and hypotension; effects may last 3 to 7 days after the last dose
Alcohol, alongside eitherAlcoholics Anonymous; motivational psychotherapy
OpioidBuprenorphine or methadone maintenance, the standard of care over withdrawal management aloneLowers relapse and fatal overdose
Opioid, buprenorphineOffice-based prescribingA low-dose start alongside the full agonist aims to avoid precipitated withdrawal
Opioid, methadoneEvaluate the patient first; use with careQTc prolongation and torsades: ECG (electrocardiogram) at start and during titration
Opioid, naltrexoneLong-acting naltrexone, from an opioid-free stateOnly after at least 7 days without a full dose of another opioid agonist
Practice
  1. 26-year-old man brought by police after fighting strangers in the street shouting that he cannot be hurt; eyes jerk up and down T 38.4 °C · BP 170/104 mm Hg · HR 118/min · pupils midsize · respirations 18/min → Intravenous lorazepam → violent agitation, vertical nystagmus and hypertension suggest PCP; benzodiazepines are the preferred sedative; urinary acidification is no longer recommended, and normal breathing with midsize pupils is not an opioid picture
  2. 29-year-old woman with chest pain an hour after a party restless, talking fast; skin wet with sweat pupils 7 mm, reactive · BP 182/106 mm Hg · HR 132/min · T 38.0 °C · no nystagmus → Cocaine intoxication → agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils and sweating form the sympathomimetic picture, and cocaine can trigger coronary ischemia; heroin gives small pupils and slow breathing
  3. 34-year-old man with chest pain and agitation after using cocaine ECG (electrocardiogram): sinus tachycardia, no ST-segment elevation; troponin pending BP 176/102 mm Hg · HR 128/min · pupils dilated · diaphoretic · oxygen saturation 98% → An intravenous benzodiazepine → benzodiazepines are first-line for cocaine agitation and cardiovascular toxicity; some clinicians avoid beta-blockers because unopposed alpha stimulation can worsen vasoconstriction
  4. 22-year-old man found unresponsive in a restroom a needle and spoon beside him; shallow, snoring respirations; no response to voice respirations 6/min · oxygen saturation 84% · pupils 1 mm · BP 104/68 mm Hg · T 36.4 °C → Naloxone → pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and decreased consciousness are the opioid triad; naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist; flumazenil is not routine and can provoke seizures
  5. 55-year-old man admitted for pancreatitis; last drink 60 hours ago now disoriented, says rats run across the floor, drenched in sweat T 38.1 °C · HR 126/min · BP 168/98 mm Hg · coarse tremor → Delirium tremens → disorientation, visual hallucinations, fever, sweating and tachycardia at 48 to 72 hours are delirium tremens, which can be fatal; hallucinosis comes earlier, at 12 to 24 hours, and opioid withdrawal after a spontaneous stop is not life-threatening
  6. 48-year-old woman 20 hours after her last drink tremulous, anxious, sweating; symptom scale score moderate needs intravenous fluids for vomiting HR 112/min · BP 152/94 mm Hg · glucose 92 mg/dL → Benzodiazepine; thiamine before glucose → benzodiazepines are first-line for moderate alcohol withdrawal, and with intravenous fluids thiamine goes before glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; clonidine is only an adjunct to a benzodiazepine
  7. 31-year-old man who stopped heroin 1 day ago yawning, runny nose, goose flesh, cramps and diarrhea wants to stop using pupils 6 mm · HR 104/min · BP 142/88 mm Hg · T 37.2 °C → Buprenorphine → opioid withdrawal after a spontaneous stop is distressing but not life-threatening; buprenorphine or methadone treats it, and clonidine can help; naloxone, an opioid antagonist, treats overdose, not withdrawal
  8. 24-year-old man with 6 months of repeated bouts of vomiting smokes cannabis daily; feels better only under hot showers normal between bouts HR 96/min · abdomen soft · lipase normal · T 36.9 °C → Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome → cyclical vomiting relieved with warm showers in daily cannabis use, which resolves with cessation; the cannabis use is the clue the other labels ignore
Pairs with Delirium: is a withdrawal driving the confusion? Psychosis: did the psychosis start during or soon after use?
Transferable rule

Pupils and breathing first: small pupils with slow breathing is an opioid; big pupils with sweating and a fast pulse is a stimulant or opioid withdrawal; nystagmus with violence is PCP.
